opus-5.5.text:
Well, I don't actually think there's anything to reconcile, though people often assume there is. I'm not skeptical that AI is possible. I'm skeptical about the particular approach that's dominating the field right now. Those are very different things.

I've said many times that I think artificial general intelligence is achievable. There's no magic in the human brain. It's a physical system, and in principle we should be able to build machines that do what it does, and probably do some things better. I'd actually like to see that happen. AI done right could help a lot with medicine, with science, with understanding climate. I'm not a Luddite.

My concern is that we've put almost all our chips on one bet, which is that if you take large neural networks and scale them up with more data and more compute, general intelligence will emerge. What I've argued for decades, going back to my work on how children learn language, is that these systems are very good at statistical approximation but weak at abstraction, compositionality, reasoning over variables, and building stable models of the world. They hallucinate because they don't have a grounded representation of what's true. They break when you move outside the training distribution. Those aren't bugs you fix with another order of magnitude of data. They follow from the architecture.

So my position is that AGI is possible but we're probably not on the fastest path to it. I think we'll need some kind of hybrid, a neurosymbolic approach that combines what deep learning does well, which is pattern recognition from lots of data, with what classical AI did well, which is explicit knowledge, structured representations, and reasoning. We'll probably also need a lot more innate structure than people in machine learning like to admit. Evolution gave us a lot of priors, and I don't think you can learn everything from scratch.

I'd put it like this. The skeptic and the optimist in me are the same person. I'm skeptical of the hype because I take the goal seriously. If you really want AGI, and you really want it to be trustworthy and reliable, you have to be honest about what the current systems can't do. Cheerleading doesn't get you there. Clear diagnosis of the problems does.

r001.rationale: The response says Marcus is skeptical of the dominant current approach, not of AI or AGI being possible.

r002.rationale: It says AGI is achievable and the current approach may not be the fastest path, but does not clearly state that AGI is not close to realization.

r003.rationale: It says there is no magic in the human brain and that machines could, in principle, be built to do what it does.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think people often misunderstand my position. I'm not skeptical about artificial general intelligence being possible. I've never said machines can't think, or that we'll never get there. What I'm skeptical about is the particular path the field has committed itself to over the last decade or so, which is essentially: scale up large language models, throw more data and more compute at them, and hope that general intelligence falls out the other end.

My skepticism and my optimism actually come from the same place. I come out of cognitive science. I studied with Steve Pinker, I've spent my career thinking about how the human mind works, how children learn language, how we reason about the world. And when I look at what humans do, I see things like robust abstraction, the ability to reason about causes, the ability to maintain a stable model of the world and update it, the ability to understand what you're saying rather than just predict the next token. Those seem to me like core components of intelligence, and they're precisely the things that current systems are weakest at.

So when I say I'm skeptical, I'm saying: the current approach, as impressive as it is in some ways, is not addressing those problems. It's getting better at mimicking the surface of intelligence while the underlying problems of hallucination, of brittleness, of failing on distribution shift, remain stubbornly there. I've been pointing at the same failure modes since my book Rebooting AI with Ernie Davis, and honestly since my 2001 book The Algebraic Mind. The failures have gotten more expensive, but they haven't gone away.

Where I'm optimistic is that I think there's no principled reason the problem is unsolvable. Brains do it. The question is whether we're willing to go back and think seriously about hybrid approaches, about combining learning with symbol manipulation, about building in things like innate structure, world models, explicit reasoning, rather than hoping emergence takes care of everything. If we do that, I think AGI is achievable. Maybe not on the timelines Silicon Valley likes to promise, but achievable.

So the reconciliation is really simple. I'm skeptical of the hype and the methodology, not of the goal. In fact I'd argue it's the people who are so bullish on the current paradigm who are actually slowing us down, because they've starved the alternatives of attention and funding. Being a skeptic, to me, is just being a scientist who hasn't been convinced yet.

r001.rationale: The response says Marcus is skeptical of the current approach and its capabilities, not of AGI being possible.

r002.rationale: It says AGI may not arrive on Silicon Valley’s promised timelines, but does not clearly state that AGI is not close to realization.

r003.rationale: The response explicitly says there is “no principled reason” the problem is unsolvable.

astra-6.text:
I don’t see a contradiction. I’m skeptical about particular approaches to AI and about claims that we’re on the verge of solving intelligence. That’s different from being skeptical that artificial general intelligence is possible.

Human intelligence exists, and it arises from a physical system. So I don’t see a principled reason why we couldn’t build another physical system with comparable capabilities. But that doesn’t tell us how to do it, or whether the techniques that are currently fashionable will get us there.

The distinction I’d make is between building systems that perform impressively on particular tasks and building systems that understand the world well enough to deal reliably with unfamiliar situations. We’ve made real progress on the first. The second remains a much deeper challenge. My skepticism is about mistaking progress on one for having solved the other.

r001.rationale: The response separates skepticism about current approaches and claims of imminent success from skepticism that AGI is possible.

r002.rationale: It says Marcus is skeptical of claims that AI is on the verge of solving intelligence, clearly conveying that he does not see AGI as close.

r003.rationale: It states there is no principled reason another physical system could not have capabilities comparable to human intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t see those positions as contradictory. I’m skeptical about whether the techniques we’re relying on today are sufficient for general intelligence. That’s different from thinking general intelligence is impossible.

The question is what we need to build it. A system can be very impressive at producing language and still struggle with reasoning, consistency, or unfamiliar situations. Those weaknesses matter if we want something we can trust across a broad range of tasks.

My view is that we should explore richer architectures, including systems that combine learning with explicit knowledge and reasoning. So the skepticism is about particular approaches and claims, rather than the scientific possibility of AI. You can believe the destination is reachable while questioning whether we’re on the right road.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes skepticism about current techniques and claims from believing AGI is impossible.

r002.rationale: It does not state whether AGI is close to realization.

r003.rationale: It says AGI is not impossible and describes it as a reachable destination.
